context: Current closing price of Caterpillar (CAT): $805.09 USD as of 2026-08-20.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I inferred was a starting price around 805–808. At the 1-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed level, expecting mean-reverting intraday dynamics with only a small positive drift, producing an estimate of 808. Over one week, I applied a slightly larger drift assumption consistent with historical equity index behavior, nudging the estimate to 812. At one month, the compounding of that drift and a longer runway for momentum or trend continuation pushed the estimate to 820. In all three cases, the point estimates are relatively close to the starting value because short-to-medium-term equity index returns have low expected drift relative to their volatility, meaning the bulk of the forecast distribution sits near the current level.

The confidence interval widths reflect the scaling of uncertainty with the square root of time, a standard feature of financial return modeling. At one day, realized volatility in equity indices is typically 0.8–1.2% per day, which maps to a roughly ±25-point band at the 90% level around 808. Over a week, that uncertainty expands proportionally, giving a ±44-point band. Over a month, the band widens to ±90 points, reflecting not just the compounding of daily volatility but also the greater chance that structural or macro factors shift the prevailing regime. I also widened the monthly interval somewhat beyond the pure square-root scaling to account for the possibility of regime changes or fat-tailed events that pure Gaussian models would underweight.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals in either direction. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward tighter financial conditions, or a geopolitical shock could trigger a risk-off selloff that moves the index well below the lower bounds, particularly at the weekly and monthly horizons. Credit stress events or a liquidity crunch in related markets could amplify such moves. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, a dovish surprise from a major central bank, or a resolution of a prevailing geopolitical tension could drive a sharp rally beyond the upper bounds. At the one-month horizon especially, the tail risks are asymmetric in practice, as markets can gap down faster than they grind up, meaning the lower tail of the actual distribution may be fatter than my symmetric intervals imply.
